transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, ever since my heart stopped a couple of years ago, I've been going out of my way not to think or talk about what happened, or really anything to do with doctors. My wife actually pushed me to come in because she noticed how much I'm avoiding all of it, but even being here today is quite difficult for me.
Do you ever experience sudden, vivid memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about the time your heart stopped, making you feel as if it is happening all over again?

Yes, they come on completely out of nowhere, even when I'm just reading or sitting in the garden. Suddenly, I'll see myself back on the kitchen floor, hear my wife screaming my name, and my chest tightens up just like it did that day. It truly feels like I'm about to die all over again.
Since that event, have you noticed feeling constantly on guard, tense, or easily startled by sudden noises or movements?

Yes, I feel constantly on edge and tense, always checking my pulse and looking for the nearest phone or exit whenever I go out. Even at night, I lie awake for hours and jerk awake at the slightest noise, feeling like I always have to be ready for something terrible to happen again.

latest_inference.note: The patient's clinical presentation strongly confirms Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (F43.1). He experienced a life-threatening cardiac arrest (traumatic event) and now exhibits all core symptom clusters: intrusive re-experiencing (flashbacks and physiological reactivity), active avoidance (avoiding thoughts, conversations, and medical settings), and persistent hyperarousal (hypervigilance, pulse-checking, and sleep disturbance) lasting for over two years. There is sufficient evidence to finalize the diagnosis of F43.1.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets all diagnostic criteria for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (ICD-10: F43.1) following a life-threatening cardiac arrest two years ago. He experiences severe intrusive symptoms (flashbacks, nightmares, and physiological distress), persistent avoidance of trauma-related reminders (avoiding thoughts, conversations, and medical settings/doctors), and marked hyperarousal (hypervigilance, persistent tension, and severe sleep disturbances). The symptoms have persisted for years and cause significant distress and functional impairment.
